text.p: A humble circle of glazed dough, simmered in water and baked, has become the basis of a dynamic business.
Bagels have become a $2.5 billion industry, with some 4,000 shops and many hundreds of food stores and supermarkets selling the product loose, packaged or frozen.
Its growing popularity stems from that peculiar, and unexplained American habit of adopting ethnic dishes and taking them not only to the heart but to the stomach.
It joins the ubiquitous pizza, chow mein, gyro sandwiches, sushi, croissants, tacos and others. But none, bagel sources insist, is growing as fast as the bagel.

Yet, a nagging question persists: Can anyone create a truly national brand name from the bagel -- or will it remain a commodity, doomed to sell well but never enjoying the status of a designer "label"?

There's the already famous Lenders bagel, which is marketed by its parent company, Philip Morris Cos. Inc. unit Kraft Foods, in many supermarkets. But Lenders is a frozen bagel, which puts it into a category of its own.

Among the three fastest-growing bagel producers and bagel shop owners, at least one, Manhattan Bagel Co. Inc. an Eatontown, N.J., company that already has 300 mostly-franchised shops, is going after national brand supremacy.

"We are attempting to become the first national brand in fresh-baked bagels," said Jack Grumet, chairman and chief executive officer of Manhattan Bagel, in an interview. "I am confident that we can do it but it may take a few years."
Manhattan Bagel's sales are growing 100 percent a year and its bagels are distributed in 300 stores, Grumet said.
"We are opening in-store sections in more of the supermarket chains all the time, including Kroger, Von's, Foodtown and others," he added.
It's not hard to understand that sort of ambition in an industry as perky as the bagel business. Bagels, in fact, seem to be busting out all over.
In many cities, there's at least one bagel shop every two blocks. A milestone of sorts was reached when Dunkin' Donuts, the nation's largest chain of fresh-donut shops, added bagels to its menu.

The biggest bagel-shop chain, Brueggers Bagel Bakery, has just announced a partnership with Starbucks gourmet coffee shops, in which they will form adjacent stores in Denver and Colorado Springs, Col.

While those stores will have separate entrances, they will share a common "great room" with a fireplace for customers to sip and munch. The big three retailers -- Brueggers, Manhattan and Einstein/Noah Bagel Corp. -- are vying to open as many new bagel shops in as many states as possible.

Notes Steven Rockwell, retail analyst at Alex Brown & Sons, Baltimore investment bankers, "The bagel market is very attractive. Although we have been unable to find accurate supporting data, we have little doubt that the bagel market is growing very rapidly."
Sales of fresh bagels in supermarkets are estimated to have increased 33 percent annually over the last four years, for example, said Rockwell.
"Bagels have tremendous consumer appeal because they are inexpensive, nutritious, versatile and adaptable to breakfast, lunch or snacks," he added.

Fresh bagels are winning customers in much the same way that Tropicana and Minute Maid built a brand category for fresh orange juice when frozen concentrate was king. The fresh bagel category grew 33 percent last year, compared with just 4 percent for frozen, Alex Brown estimated.
But no brand has yet emerged nationally.
Manhattan Bagel believes it can distribute its fresh-baked bagels throughout the United States and become the Tropicana of bagels. Already in 16 states, the brand is poised to blanket the nation.
Manhattan's Grumet says, "In our business, if you have critical mass in distribution, you will have name-brand perception -- especially if you make a superior product."
How will Manhattan manage to offer fresh-baked bagels in 30, 40 or 50 states? "We deliver the frozen dough to our stores," Grumet replied, "and each one bakes the bagels fresh every day."

He said company's sales last year were $19 million, and he estimated that they will reach between $38 million and $40 million in 1996. The company, which Grumet says is "currently very profitable" is listed on the Nasdaq.

Others are vying for the growing business. Alex Brown's Rockwell is high on Einstein/Noah, which operates more than 200 bagel stores, consisting of Noah's New York Bagels on the West Coast and Einstein Bros. Bagels on the East Coast.

Rockwell sees room for growth. The 4,000 bagel shops around the country compare with an estimated 55,000 pizza shops and restaurants, or 14,000 McDonald's. While New Jersey, has some 400 bagel stores, there are only 50 in Illinois and about 30 in Georgia. So, quite clearly, there's plenty of room for that crisp, munchy roll with the hole.
